PAPER: JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH Golbus et al Original Paper Impact of Push Notifications on Physical Activity and Sodium Intake Among Patients with Hypertension: Microrandomized Trial of a Just-in-Time Adaptive Intervention Jessica R Golbus1,2*, MD, MS; Michael P Dorsch3*, MS, PharmD; Yuxuan Chen4, MS; Tanima Basu1, MA, MS; Evan Luff1, MS; Predrag Klasnja5, PhD; Mark W Newman5, PhD; Lesli E Skolarus6, MD, MS; Walter Dempsey4, PhD; Brahmajee K Nallamothu1,2, MPH, MD 1Division of Cardiovascular Medicine, Department of Internal Medicine, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, United States 2Michigan Integrated Center for Health Analytics and Medical Prediction (MiCHAMP), University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, United States 3Department of Clinical Pharmacy, College of Pharmacy, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, United States 4Department of Biostatistics, University of Michigan School of Public Health, Ann Arbor, MI, United States 5School of Information and Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, United States 6Division of Stroke Vascular Neurology, Davee Department of Neurology, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, Chicago, IL, United States *these authors contributed equally Corresponding Author: Jessica R Golbus, MD, MS Division of Cardiovascular Medicine, Department of Internal Medicine University of Michigan 2723 Cardiovascular Center, 1500 E Medical Center Dr. SPC 5853 Ann Arbor, MI 48109 United States Phone: 1 7342325045 Email: jgolbus@med.umich.edu Abstract Background: Achieving adequate blood pressure control is challenging for patients and clinicians. Digital hypertension management solutions that use push notifications to promote lifestyle management have been proposed as an approach, but their effectiveness remains unknown. Objective: This analysis was designed to interrogate the independent and short-term effects of push notifications, tailored to participant and environmental factors, and on physical activity levels and sodium intake among individuals with hypertension. Methods: The myBPmyLife study was a 6-month randomized controlled trial of participants with self-reported hypertension recruited from an academic medical center and federally qualified health centers. A core component of the intervention consisted of microrandomized push notifications promoting lifestyle modifications that were randomly delivered at 4 daily time points and focused on physical activity and dietary sodium intake. Our primary outcome for this secondary analysis was the step count 60 minutes after a physical activity notification and lower-sodium food choices 24 hours after a dietary notification. This analysis focuses on the results of the microrandomized trial and used a centered and weighted least squares method adapted for 2 or more treatments. Results: A total of 298 participants were randomized to the intervention arm, of whom 287 had data available for analysis. Participants’ mean age was 59.5 (SD 13.1) years, 138 (48.1%) were women, and 206 (71.8%) were White. Participants were randomized at 187,517 time points over 6 months, which led to 0.96 (SD 0.86) push notifications per day divided between activity (50.4%; SD 0.4) and dietary (49.8%; SD 0.4) notifications. Activity notifications did not increase step count in the 60 minutes after a notification (estimate 1.01, 95% CI 0.98‐1.04; P=.40). Similarly, dietary notifications did not impact the number of lower-sodium food choices in the subsequent 24 hours (estimate 0.93, 95% CI 0.83‐1.04; P=.23), but in exploratory post hoc analyses, did increase mobile app use by 95.5% (95% CI 1.81‐2.10; P<.001), mobile app clicks or searches by 93.7% (95% CI 1.72%‐2.16%; P<.001), and low sodium searches by 113.0% (95% CI 1.73‐2.53; P<.001), all within 60 minutes. JSON: Name: mrt_push_notifications_hypertension Title: Microrandomized trial evaluation of contextually tailored push notifications to increase short-term physical activity and lower-sodium food choices among adults with hypertension Short Hypothesis: Contextually tailored push notifications causally increase proximal healthy behaviors: activity notifications increase mean step count in the 60 minutes after delivery and dietary notifications increase the number of lower-sodium food choices within 24 hours, compared to no notification. Related Work: Digital hypertension interventions have combined home blood-pressure self-monitoring, medication management, and mobile app–delivered behavior-change components. Prior randomized trials showed reductions in systolic blood pressure when self-monitoring was paired with intensive co-interventions, but the independent causal effects of push notifications remain unresolved. Existing studies that evaluate notifications either assess distal outcomes only or use heterogeneous notification framings and limited tailoring. Microrandomized trials provide a rigorous framework to estimate proximal causal effects, but few have been applied to hypertension and lifestyle mediators; prior microrandomized studies often use narrow tailoring variables, small samples, limited handling of zero-inflated behavioral outcomes, and sparse mediation analyses to link engagement to downstream outcomes. Open gaps include optimal tailoring dimensions (contextual, psychosocial, temporal), appropriate proximal outcome windows, and methods for estimating causal excursion effects in the presence of zero-inflation and repeated treatments. Abstract: Problem: The independent, short-term causal effects of push notifications on physical activity and lower-sodium food choices among adults with hypertension are unclear. Approach: Using a microrandomized trial framework embedded in a multicomponent mobile health intervention, evaluate proximal causal effects of contextually tailored activity and dietary push notifications on step counts within 60 minutes and lower-sodium choices within 24 hours. Main contribution: (1) a reproducible experimental pipeline that estimates causal excursion effects using weighted and centered least squares adapted for multiple treatments and zero-inflated outcomes, (2) prespecified moderator and mediation analyses to identify subgroups and to test whether immediate engagement mediates downstream behavior change, and (3) an ablation comparing tailored, generic, and reinforcement-learning delivery strategies. Expected outcome: Quantified proximal effects, identification of moderators (eg, baseline activity, age), and evidence whether increased app engagement mediates longer-term changes in activity and sodium intake, informing notification design in hypertension management. Experiments: Datasets: Primary: myBPmyLife microrandomized trial dataset (intervention arm, N≈287, decision points≈187,517) including timestamped push delivery logs, smartwatch heart rate and step counts, mobile app logs (opens, clicks, searches), Block sodium screener, baseline demographics, and 6-month outcomes. Secondary: replication dataset from an independent hypertension mHealth cohort if available. Baselines: (A) no-notification (available but not randomized) decision points, (B) generic non-tailored notification, (C) app-only engagement (no push), and (D) reinforcement-learning–personalized delivery (simulated/offline RL policy applied to logged data). Primary outcomes: mean step count within 60 minutes post decision point (log-transformed after +0.5), and count of lower-sodium food choices recorded in app within 24 hours (zero-inflated count). Secondary outcomes: app open within 60 minutes (binary), number of searches/clicks within 60 minutes (count), low-sodium searches within 60 minutes (count), 7-day aggregated daily steps, 6-month self-reported sodium intake, and 6-month systolic BP. Statistical methods: estimate causal excursion effects using weighted and centered least squares (WCLS) adapted for ≥2 treatments for step outcome; use zero-inflated generalized estimating equations or the Liu et al. approach for dietary counts; apply inverse probability weighting for availability and message delivery. Prespecified analyses: (1) main effect tests for activity and dietary notifications vs no-notification; (2) moderator analyses (interaction terms) for baseline activity (dichotomized at mean), age (<65/≥65), gender, and site; (3) mediation analysis testing app engagement (app open within 60 min) as mediator between dietary notifications and 24-hour low-sodium choices using causal mediation methods for time-varying mediators; (4) time-varying treatment effect modeling (quadratic and spline terms) to estimate decay/learning; (5) sensitivity analyses excluding decision points with missing wear-time in 3 hours post-notification and analysis restricted to smartwatch-only vs phone-only data; (6) ablation: compare tailored notification set vs non-tailored and offline RL policy vs microrandomized estimates; (7) multiple testing correction using false discovery rate (Benjamini-Hochberg) within primary and secondary families. Evaluation metrics and reporting: effect estimates with 95% CIs and p-values, percent change interpretations for exponentiated models, model fit statistics (AIC/BIC), and proportion of variance explained for mediation. Reproducibility: share analysis scripts and pre-registered analysis plan; report decision-point counts, availability rates, and missing-data patterns. Risk Factors and Limitations: Selection bias toward smartphone owners and relatively active, health-engaged participants limits external validity. Measurement error from smartwatch step undercounting or missingness and from self-reported app food-choice logging creates noise and potential misclassification. Push-notification delivery failures, OS-level suppression, or delayed delivery may bias estimates toward the null. Zero-inflated dietary outcomes and sparse events reduce power and complicate model assumptions. Small marginal effect sizes may require larger samples to detect; existing dataset may be underpowered for small proximal effects and some subgroup interactions. Time-varying confounding from unmeasured stimuli (other apps, social interactions) may bias causal estimates. Generalization to populations with higher uncontrolled BP, different socioeconomic status, or different device ecosystems is limited. Multiple hypothesis testing across outcomes and moderators increases false-positive risk if not controlled. Causal mediation with time-varying mediator and exposures relies on sequential ignorability assumptions that may be violated.
